title: India–China: Border and Strategy

cards.b:
India–China has appeared in the PSIR paper almost every year since 2015. It is the central security question for India. It is also the one with the most dates, treaties and places to remember.

This lesson covers the border and strategy: where the dispute lies, how the 1993–2013 agreements tried to manage it, what Galwan changed, and how the 2024–26 thaw works. The next lesson covers economy and multilateral rivalry.

Core tension: China wants a stable border so that it can deal with India as one of many partners. India says that peace on the border is the basis of the whole relationship. After Galwan (2020), India made normal ties conditional on restoring the border status quo.

cards.h: The three sectors of the dispute
cards.b:
The border is about 3,488 km by India's count (China says about 2,000). It is the Line of Actual Control (LAC), not a settled boundary. The term was used in a 1959 letter from Zhou Enlai and written into the 1993 agreement.

The McMahon Line comes from the 1914 Simla Convention. China does not accept it. It calls Arunachal "South Tibet". China also holds the Shaksgam Valley that Pakistan ceded to it in 1963. Both sides have different perceptions of where the LAC runs, so patrols often meet face to face.

Nehru's forward policy (1961) put small Indian posts in disputed territory. China answered with a large attack in October 1962. It declared a unilateral ceasefire in November. India lost the war, and the shock still shapes its military thinking.

Ties were restored step by step. Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit to Beijing started a "delink" approach: improve other ties while talking about the border.

cards.h: The agreements that kept the peace
cards.b:
Between 1993 and 2013 India and China built a rulebook for the LAC.

  • 1993 Agreement on Maintenance of Peace and Tranquillity along the LAC.
  • 1996 Agreement on Confidence-Building Measures in the military field. It bars use of firearms and explosives within 2 km of the LAC. This is why Galwan was fought with rods and stones.
  • 2005 Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for settling the boundary. Both sides should keep settled populations in mind.
  • 2012 WMCC (Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination).
  • 2013 Border Defence Cooperation Agreement (BDCA).

The Special Representatives (SR) mechanism began in 2003. The SRs are India's NSA and China's Foreign Minister.

Doklam (June–August 2017): China began building a road on the Doklam plateau, claimed by Bhutan, near the tri-junction. Indian troops crossed to stop it. The 73-day standoff ended on 28 August with both sides pulling back. Doklam is near the Siliguri Corridor, India's 'chicken's neck'.

Galwan (15 June 2020): after Chinese build-up in Eastern Ladakh from May 2020, a violent clash in the Galwan Valley killed 20 Indian soldiers. China later acknowledged four of its own dead. It was the first deadly clash since 1975.

China also occupied points at Pangong Tso, Gogra-Hot Springs, Depsang and Demchok. Both sides sent about 50,000–60,000 troops each into the theatre.

India responded with a ban on Chinese apps, tighter FDI rules (Press Note 3, April 2020) and a military build-up.

Talks went through Corps Commander rounds and the WMCC. At several points both sides created buffer zones, where neither patrols. India lost some patrolling rights this way, critics say.

The October 2024 agreement let patrols resume at Depsang Plains and Demchok. Disengagement was done; de-escalation and de-induction of troops (pulling back the heavy deployments) are still pending, as of 2026.

After Kazan the two sides rebuilt step by step.

  • December 2024: 23rd SR talks in Beijing (Doval and Wang Yi).
  • 2025: Kailash Mansarovar Yatra resumed; Wang Yi visited Delhi for the 24th SR round in August; Modi met Xi at the SCO summit in Tianjin (31 August–1 September) and both said they are partners, not rivals.
  • Late 2025: direct flights restarted after five years; border trade through Lipulekh, Shipki La and Nathu La was agreed.
  • August 2026: the 25th SR round in Beijing reportedly agreed more military meeting points and hotlines and a group to delimit the less disputed parts of the border. The next round is due in India in 2027.

Analysts call this "normalisation without trust": a managed truce, not a settlement.

cards.h: China's pressure points beyond the LAC
cards.b:
• Water: China began building a huge dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra) near the great bend in 2025. India plans the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project in reply.
  • Renaming: China keeps issuing 'standardised' Chinese names for places in Arunachal.
  • Tibet and the Dalai Lama: China insists on approving his reincarnation. The Dalai Lama said in July 2025 that the institution will continue. India says it takes no position on religious succession.
  • Pakistan: China arms Pakistan (J-10C jets, PL-15 missiles) and backs CPEC through PoK. Indian officials said China gave support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor in May 2025.
  • Indian Ocean: Chinese research ships, the Djibouti base (2017), Gwadar and Hambantota, the so-called 'string of pearls'.

India's counters: the Vibrant Villages Programme, border roads and tunnels (Atal Tunnel, Sela Tunnel 2024), the Andaman and Nicobar command, the Quad and Malabar.

Jaishankar's formula for ties is the three mutuals: mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest. India links progress to peace on the LAC. China prefers to put the border "in its appropriate place" and widen cooperation elsewhere.

Scholars differ. Shivshankar Menon (Choices, 2016) sees management and deterrence. Others, such as Tanvi Madan (Fateful Triangle, 2020), see India hedging between the US and China.

Policy options India uses at once: deterrence (troop posture, infrastructure), diplomacy (SR talks, WMCC), partnerships (Quad, France, Japan, Vietnam, Philippines BrahMos sale) and economic caution (apps, FDI screening).

It also keeps both doors open: Modi visited China in 2025 for the SCO while India hosted BRICS in 2026.

For the exam, link the border to Tibet policy (India recognised the Tibet Autonomous Region as part of China in 2003; China implicitly accepted Sikkim as Indian in 2003–04 by agreeing to trade through Nathu La), to Bhutan (Doklam) and to Nepal (Lipulekh).

Structure: (1) sectors and the LAC; (2) 1914, 1954, 1962; (3) the 1993–2013 rulebook; (4) Doklam and Galwan; (5) disengagement and the October 2024 pact; (6) 2025–26 thaw and what is unresolved (de-escalation, buffer zones, water, Tibet); (7) way forward.

quiz.q: The McMahon Line is the boundary drawn in:
quiz.w: Sir Henry McMahon drew it at the 1914 Simla Convention; China rejects it.

quiz.q: The 1996 CBM agreement prohibits firearms and explosives within what distance of the LAC?
quiz.w: Within 2 km of the LAC. This explains the stones-and-rods clash at Galwan.

quiz.q: The Galwan clash took place on:
The Doklam standoff of 2017 lasted about:
The October 2024 India-China arrangement mainly covered patrolling at:
quiz.w: It restored patrolling at Depsang Plains and Demchok, the last two friction points.

quiz.q: The Special Representatives mechanism on the boundary began in:
quiz.w: Established in 2003 during Vajpayee's visit to China.

quiz.q: The 2005 agreement on boundary settlement is called:
quiz.w: The 2005 Political Parameters and Guiding Principles. BDCA is 2013; the 1993 agreement is on peace and tranquillity.

quiz.q: Which stretch did Pakistan cede to China in 1963?
quiz.w: Pakistan ceded the Shaksgam Valley under the 1963 boundary agreement with China.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the 'three mutuals' in Jaishankar's formula?
quiz.w: The three mutuals are respect, sensitivity and interest.

quiz.q: Where did Modi and Xi meet in October 2024, soon after the patrolling agreement?
quiz.w: At the BRICS summit in Kazan on 23 October 2024. Wuhan was 2018, Mamallapuram 2019, Tianjin 2025.
